samples.summary: Google sign-up crashes (500) and leaves an orphaned user row when the display-name-derived workspace slug collides
samples.evidence: `AuthController.googleAuthCallback` (auth.controller.ts:280) calls `findOrCreateUser({ username: googleUser.username, ... })` where `username` is now `profile.displayName` (google.strategy.ts:75), which is NOT unique and NOT restricted to ASCII. `findOrCreateUser` derives the workspace slug naively: `newUser.username.toLowerCase().replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g,'-').replace(/^-+|-+$/g,'') + '-s-workspace'` (user.service.ts:54-58) and `Workspace.slug` is `@unique` (schema.prisma:168). So (a) any non-Latin display name (e.g. '홍길동', '李') reduces to the empty base and yields the single slug `-s-workspace`, and (b) two Google accounts named 'John Smith', or the email-local-part fallback for ada@a.com and ada@b.com, yield identical slugs. The second such signup: `prisma.user.create` succeeds, then `prisma.workspace.create` throws P2002 — there is no transaction and no catch anywhere up to the controller — so the request 500s and the user row survives with no workspace, permanently broken (the retry now takes the existing-user branch and never creates a workspace). This was previously unreachable because GitHub `username` is a globally-unique ASCII login. The codebase already knows this hazard: `WorkspaceService.generateUniqueSlug` (workspace.service.ts:22, 277-281) dedupes and falls back to a neutral base for exactly the empty-slug case; `findOrCreateUser` does not use it.

samples.summary: New verified-email requirement refuses GitHub logins whenever passport-github2's /user/emails fetch does not supply flags, including on the documented GitHub Enterprise setup
samples.evidence: `verifiedEmail()` (github.strategy.ts:57-64) now requires `e.verified` to be affirmatively set, and `validate` throws `UnauthorizedException` otherwise (line 132). But `profile.emails` is not always the raw `/user/emails` list: passport-github2 falls back to the address parsed out of `GET /user` (which carries no `verified` flag) whenever the email request errors or returns nothing — which is exactly the GHE misconfiguration this file's own comment at lines 76-78 documents (a GHE token hitting api.github.com fails with 'Bad credentials'). Previously such a deployment still logged in via `emails?.[0]?.value`; now every login is refused. It is also a hard fail-closed on any transient GitHub API hiccup, converting a working login into a 401.

samples.summary: Refusal from validate() surfaces as raw backend JSON with no route back to the login page
samples.evidence: `GitHubStrategy.validate` (line 133) and `GoogleStrategy.validate` (google.strategy.ts:115,119) throw `UnauthorizedException`, which `AuthGuard` turns into a 401 JSON body on the BACKEND origin. Every other refusal on these callbacks deliberately redirects to `${FRONTEND_URL}/login?error=...` for the reason spelled out in auth.controller.ts:142-150 ('a raw Nest error page on the backend origin leaves the user staring at JSON with no way back'). The same dead end applies when the user declines Google consent (`?error=access_denied` makes passport `fail()` → 401 JSON). Users hitting the new verified-email refusal get no retry path.

samples.summary: Google callback leaves the OAuth state cookie uncleared on the early-refusal branches
samples.evidence: The `||` chain at auth.controller.ts:265-271 short-circuits: when `stateToken` is not a string or `isWebOAuthState(stateToken)` is false, `consumeWebOAuthState` never runs, so `res.clearCookie(oauthStateCookieName(), ...)` is skipped and the state secret survives its failed login for the full 10-minute `STATE_COOKIE_MAX_AGE_MS`. `consumeWebOAuthState`'s own doc (web-oauth-login.ts:60-61) states the cookie is cleared 'whether or not it matches, so a failed login leaves nothing behind to replay'; these two branches break that invariant.

samples.summary: resolveEmail only ever inspects emails[0], so a profile whose first address is unverified is refused even when a verified one follows
samples.evidence: `const entry = profile.emails?.[0]` (google.strategy.ts:54) and `email = entry?.value ?? claims?.email` — if `emails[0]` is present but unverified, `email` is fixed to that address and `_json.email` is only consulted for flags when it equals it, so `validate` throws even though a verified address exists later in the array. The GitHub side deliberately does the opposite (`verifiedEmail` scans the whole list and falls back to any verified address, github.strategy.ts:59-62); the two merge points are inconsistent and the Google one can lock out an account it should admit.

samples.summary: Adding GOOGLE_CALLBACK_URL to the secure-cookie probe can silently flip an existing production deployment's cookies to non-Secure
samples.evidence: `isSecureCookie()` now loops over `['GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL','GOOGLE_CALLBACK_URL']` (oauth-state.ts:244-248). A deployment that today configures no `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL` and relies on the `NODE_ENV === 'production'` fallback (line 249) will, the moment an operator adds an `http://` `GOOGLE_CALLBACK_URL` (e.g. copied from the self-hosting docs behind a TLS-terminating proxy), start minting session, refresh and state cookies without `Secure` and without `__Host-`, and existing `__Host-` sessions stop being recognised (the read side uses the same name function), logging everyone out. The 'GitHub first' ordering does not cover this case because GitHub's variable is unset.

finding.summary: Google sign-up crashes (500) and leaves an orphaned user row when the display-name-derived workspace slug collides
finding.evidence: `AuthController.googleAuthCallback` (auth.controller.ts:280) calls `findOrCreateUser({ username: googleUser.username, ... })` where `username` is now `profile.displayName` (google.strategy.ts:75), which is NOT unique and NOT restricted to ASCII. `findOrCreateUser` derives the workspace slug naively: `newUser.username.toLowerCase().replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g,'-').replace(/^-+|-+$/g,'') + '-s-workspace'` (user.service.ts:54-58) and `Workspace.slug` is `@unique` (schema.prisma:168). So (a) any non-Latin display name (e.g. '홍길동', '李') reduces to the empty base and yields the single slug `-s-workspace`, and (b) two Google accounts named 'John Smith', or the email-local-part fallback for ada@a.com and ada@b.com, yield identical slugs. The second such signup: `prisma.user.create` succeeds, then `prisma.workspace.create` throws P2002 — there is no transaction and no catch anywhere up to the controller — so the request 500s and the user row survives with no workspace, permanently broken (the retry now takes the existing-user branch and never creates a workspace). This was previously unreachable because GitHub `username` is a globally-unique ASCII login. The codebase already knows this hazard: `WorkspaceService.generateUniqueSlug` (workspace.service.ts:22, 277-281) dedupes and falls back to a neutral base for exactly the empty-slug case; `findOrCreateUser` does not use it.

verdict.reason: All claims verified in the repo. user.service.ts:54-58 derives the workspace slug naively (lowercase, non-alphanumerics to '-', trim) with no uniqueness check and no empty-base fallback, while schema.prisma:168 declares `slug String @unique`. user.service.ts:50-64 creates the User first and the Workspace second with no `$transaction` and no try/catch, so a P2002 on the workspace insert leaves a committed, workspace-less user; the early return at user.service.ts:46-48 means every retry takes the existing-user branch, making the orphan permanent. google.strategy.ts:74-76 sets `username` to `profile.displayName?.trim() || email.split('@')[0]` — non-unique and not ASCII-restricted — and auth.controller.ts:280-285 feeds it straight into `findOrCreateUser` with no catch in the chain. Both collision modes are real: an all-CJK display name reduces to the empty base yielding the single slug `-s-workspace`, and two 'John Smith' accounts (or `ada@a.com`/`ada@b.com` fallbacks) produce identical slugs. No global P2002 filter covers this path (grep found P2002 handling only in workspace.service.ts:197 and lakehouse.service.ts:1705), so the callback 500s. The codebase's own workspace.service.ts:275-287 `generateUniqueSlug` handles exactly these two cases and is used by `create` (line 22) but not by `findOrCreateUser`. Crash on a real sign-up path plus permanently inconsistent persisted state — squarely in the correctness lane and blocking.

finding.summary: New verified-email requirement refuses GitHub logins whenever passport-github2's /user/emails fetch does not supply flags, including on the documented GitHub Enterprise setup
finding.evidence: `verifiedEmail()` (github.strategy.ts:57-64) now requires `e.verified` to be affirmatively set, and `validate` throws `UnauthorizedException` otherwise (line 132). But `profile.emails` is not always the raw `/user/emails` list: passport-github2 falls back to the address parsed out of `GET /user` (which carries no `verified` flag) whenever the email request errors or returns nothing — which is exactly the GHE misconfiguration this file's own comment at lines 76-78 documents (a GHE token hitting api.github.com fails with 'Bad credentials'). Previously such a deployment still logged in via `emails?.[0]?.value`; now every login is refused. It is also a hard fail-closed on any transient GitHub API hiccup, converting a working login into a 401.

verdict.reason: The finding's load-bearing claim - that the documented GitHub Enterprise setup now fails - is contradicted by the file itself. The documented GHE configuration (github.strategy.ts:70-75) sets all four vars including GITHUB_USER_EMAIL_URL=https://ghe.example.com/api/v3/user/emails; the comment at :76-78 exists precisely to instruct that override (it describes the consequence of NOT setting it, not a supported setup). github.strategy.spec.ts:43-58 and :108-119 pin that the email endpoint is honoured and independently overridable, so a documented GHE deployment fetches /user/emails from GHE with verified/primary flags intact and verifiedEmail() resolves normally. The remaining half - a passport-github2 fallback after an email-fetch error yielding flagless emails and thus a 401 - is not a logic error but explicitly designed, documented and test-pinned behavior: github.strategy.ts:32-56 and :128-131 state the rationale (findOrCreateUser matches on email alone, so an unverified address is a path into an account created via Google), docs/design/backend.md:899-907 records it as a load-bearing invariant, and github.strategy.spec.ts:166-176 asserts refusal for exactly the 'nothing verified' and 'no emails field' shapes such a fallback would produce. Under the correctness rubric the condition is not inverted, off-by-one, or an unguarded crash: on a transient upstream failure the login fails loudly and early with an actionable message and is retryable, with no crash, data loss, or inconsistent state left behind. Acting on the finding would mean reintroducing the sign-in-on-unverified-address hole the check exists to close.

finding.summary: Google strategy registration is decided at module-import time, before ConfigModule loads `.env` — a `.env`-configured deployment advertises Google but 500s on `/auth/google`
finding.evidence: `const googleProviders = googleAuthConfigured() ? [GoogleStrategy] : [];` (auth.module.ts:37) runs when the module file is *evaluated*, which is before the `@Module({ imports: [ConfigModule.forRoot(), ...] })` decorator below it (and before AppModule's `ConfigModule.forRoot({isGlobal:true})`, since app.module.ts imports auth.module.ts first). `oauth-providers.ts` reads `process.env` only. The backend's documented configuration mechanism is a `.env` file in the package (packages/backend/README.md:18 'Create a `.env` file in this package'), and `nest start` does not preload dotenv (packages/backend/package.json scripts have no `-r dotenv/config`). So with GOOGLE_* set only in `.env`, `googleAuthConfigured()` is false at line 37 and `GoogleStrategy` is never provided — yet `AuthController.authProviders()` (auth.controller.ts:240) and `assertGoogleConfigured()` (google-auth.guard.ts) evaluate the same function *per request*, after ConfigModule populated `process.env`, so both report/allow Google. Result: the login page shows the Google button, the guard lets the request through, and `AuthGuard('google')` fails with passport's `Unknown authentication strategy "google"` → 500 on every Google sign-in attempt. The half-configured boot warning also never fires, because all three vars *are* set at that later point.

verdict.reason: The finding's central evidence — `const googleProviders = googleAuthConfigured() ? [GoogleStrategy] : [];` evaluated at module-scope (auth.module.ts:37) — does not exist in this repository. Grepping the whole tree, the only occurrence of that expression is at packages/backend/src/auth/auth.module.ts:37, and it is *inside a JSDoc comment* (the comment block spans lines 26–54) that explicitly explains why that approach was rejected, reciting exactly the failure mode the reviewer describes. The real registration is packages/backend/src/auth/auth.module.ts:55-60: `const googleStrategyProvider = { provide: GoogleStrategy, useFactory: (configService: ConfigService) => googleAuthConfigured() ? new GoogleStrategy(configService) : null, inject: [ConfigService] }`, listed in `providers` at line 85. A `useFactory` body runs during injector instantiation, i.e. after `ConfigModule.forRoot()` (line 64) and AppModule's global ConfigModule have populated `process.env` from `.env`, so it reads the same environment state that `AuthController.authProviders()` (auth.controller.ts:240) and `google-auth.guard.ts:22` read per request. The `AuthModule` constructor holding the half-configured warning (lines 97-105) likewise runs at instantiation, not at import, so the "warning never fires" corollary also rests on the absent code. No timing skew exists as described; the described divergence between advertised provider, guard, and passport registry is not reachable from this code.

finding.summary: `emailIsVerified` validates a verification flag that may belong to a different address than the email actually used
finding.evidence: `validate` picks `email = profile.emails?.[0]?.value ?? profile._json?.email` (line 73), but `emailIsVerified` accepts when *either* `profile.emails[0].verified === true` **or** `profile._json.email_verified === true` (lines 23-26). The two signals are not tied to the same address: if a profile ever carries an `emails[0]` distinct from `_json.email`, an unverified `emails[0]` is accepted on the strength of `_json.email_verified`, and since `findOrCreateUser` matches on email alone (user.service.ts:41-45) that signs the holder into whatever account owns the unverified address. The verification check should be evaluated against the address that is actually used.

verdict.reason: The finding describes a function `emailIsVerified` that accepts a flat OR of `profile.emails[0].verified === true || profile._json.email_verified === true`; no such function exists (grep for `emailIsVerified` returns zero matches repo-wide). The real code, `resolveEmail()` in packages/backend/src/auth/google.strategy.ts:49-64, ties each verification flag to the address it belongs to: it resolves `email = entry?.value ?? claims?.email` (line 55), then pushes `entry.verified` only `if (entry?.value === email)` (line 59) and the `_json` claims only `if (claims?.email === email)` (lines 60-62), before `verified: flags.some(isVerifiedFlag)` (line 63). Therefore a verified `_json.email` can never vouch for a different, unverified `emails[0]`; validate() throws UnauthorizedException on `!verified` (lines 118-123) before anything reaches findOrCreateUser. The file's doc comment (lines 38-47) names the flat-OR form as the rejected prior shape, and google.strategy.spec.ts:136-147 explicitly asserts the mismatched-address case is refused. The cited line numbers also do not match the file (lines 20-29 are isVerifiedFlag/GoogleClaims; line 73 is JSDoc).

finding.summary: Strict `=== true` on `email_verified` refuses the sign-in if Google returns the claim as a string
finding.evidence: `profile.emails?.[0]?.verified === true || profile._json?.email_verified === true`. Google's userinfo has historically returned `email_verified`/`verified_email` as the string `"true"` in some response shapes, and `passport-google-oauth20` copies the raw JSON value onto `emails[].verified` without coercion. A string value makes both comparisons false and every Google login is refused with `UnauthorizedException('Google account email is not verified')` — the feature fails closed for all users, with no way for the operator to fix it.

verdict.reason: The finding's quoted evidence (`profile.emails?.[0]?.verified === true || profile._json?.email_verified === true`) does not exist in the repository. The actual code at packages/backend/src/auth/google.strategy.ts:20-22 defines `isVerifiedFlag(value)` returning `value === true || (typeof value === 'string' && value.trim().toLowerCase() === 'true')`, which explicitly coerces the string `"true"` case- and whitespace-insensitively — precisely the scenario the finding says is unhandled. The doc comment at lines 8-19 names this exact Google userinfo string-valued-claim hazard as the reason the strict comparison was replaced. resolveEmail (lines 58-63) applies `flags.some(isVerifiedFlag)` across `entry.verified`, `claims.email_verified`, and `claims.verified_email` (including the legacy `verified_email` spelling), so a string flag from any shape satisfies verification and the UnauthorizedException at lines 118-123 is not reached. A repo-wide grep for `email_verified === true` / `verified === true` under packages/ returns no matches, confirming the strict comparison is absent everywhere, not just at the cited file.
